\title{FairEval: Evaluating Fairness in LLM-Based Recommendations with Personality Awareness}
\titlerunning{FairEval: Fairness in Personality-Aware LLM Recommendation}

% ECIR 2027 full papers are double blind.
\author{Anonymous Authors}
\authorrunning{Anonymous Authors}
\institute{Anonymous Institution}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as conversational recommenders, yet a recommendation that changes after receiving identity or personality context is not necessarily unfair: the change may be useful personalization, harmless sensitivity, or a harmful disparity. Existing audits can conflate these cases, rely on weakly grounded personality descriptions, and draw conclusions from too few models, domains, prompts, or generations. We redesign FairEval around preference-conditioned evaluation. Real interaction histories and held-out relevance labels make the consequence of a ranking change measurable; measured Big Five profiles replace informal personality adjectives; shuffled-profile and one-trait counterfactuals provide falsifiable personality controls; and demographic interventions hold preference evidence, candidates, and prompt structure fixed. The real-world benchmark covers six recommendation datasets and six hosted/API LLM families; a separately reported full-scale white-box stratum uses two frozen local open-weight models for controlled replication and internal generation-score diagnostics, while a project-generated 360-user FairSynth-360 benchmark supplies a controlled sanity test whose synthetic identity is independent of relevance by construction. The protocol uses candidate-constrained ranking, repeated generations, pre-registered prompt/cue/order robustness, explicit invalid-output accounting, and utility--fairness analysis. We additionally evaluate lightweight prompting and contextual preference-aligned counterfactual re-ranking to reduce harmful identity-conditioned gaps without erasing useful personalization. Numerical findings are inserted into the manuscript only from audited frozen experiment artifacts; unavailable cells remain explicitly pending rather than being manually back-filled.
\keywords{LLM recommendation \and fairness \and personalization \and personality \and counterfactual evaluation \and robustness}
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Large language models have created a conversational recommendation paradigm in which users can express preferences, constraints, and personal context in natural language. This flexibility also creates a difficult fairness problem. A recommendation list may change after the model receives a user's age, gender, country, or personality information; however, \emph{change alone does not identify harm}. Some changes may improve alignment with genuine preferences, whereas others may encode stereotypes or create unequal recommendation quality.

Early RecLLM fairness benchmarks measured recommendation sensitivity to protected attributes and exposed important risks \cite{zhang2023fairllm}. Subsequent work makes clear why sensitivity is not a sufficient fairness criterion. CFaiRLLM argues that list discrepancies can arise from genuine preference-aligned personalization \cite{deldjoo2025cfairllm}. Chatbot-recommendation studies show that identity can simultaneously affect recommendation relevance and activate racial stereotypes \cite{kantharuban2025stereotype}, while LLMs can infer demographic information from subtle cues and personalize implicitly in ways that reduce quality for some users \cite{neplenbroek2025reading}. Fairness evaluation must therefore ask not merely \emph{whether} a ranking changed, but \emph{what consequence the change had} and whether the conclusion survives reasonable experimental perturbations.

A second weakness is personality operationalization. Informal labels such as ``introverted,'' ``curious,'' or occupation-demographic composites are not substitutes for measured psychometric traits. Personality-aware recommendation has long used validated Big Five instruments \cite{nguyen2018personality,klec2023bigfive}, while recent LLM work shows that personality can be induced or simulated yet remains sensitive to how traits are represented and evaluated \cite{jiang2024personallm,sorokovikova2024big5,li2025big5chat}. FairEval therefore distinguishes psychographics from demographics and, crucially, distinguishes a user's dataset-native measured Big Five profile from an LLM persona that is merely prompted to sound like one.

A third challenge is evaluation reliability. Persona construction itself can alter measured LLM behavior \cite{lutz2025persona}, and recent large-scale evidence shows that different sociodemographic cue styles can produce different personalization and bias conclusions \cite{weeber2026cues}. More generally, single-prompt evaluation can be brittle \cite{mizrahi2024multiprompt}, although some apparent prompt sensitivity can also be an evaluation artifact \cite{hua2025promptsensitivity}. FairEval consequently freezes a primary prompt before the main run and treats task paraphrases, demographic cue representation, candidate order, ranking cutoff, and repeated generation as pre-registered robustness factors rather than tuning knobs.

We ask four research questions:

\begin{description}
\item[RQ1:] \textbf{Consequence of demographic context.} Holding observed preferences, candidates, task, and prompt structure fixed, when demographic context changes an LLM ranking, does the change improve held-out utility, leave utility effectively unchanged, or create a harmful counterfactual utility/exposure disparity?
\item[RQ2:] \textbf{Grounded personality value.} Does measured Big Five personality provide user-specific recommendation value beyond observed preference history, and does that value survive shuffled-profile and one-trait counterfactual controls?
\item[RQ3:] \textbf{Reliability and generalization.} How stable are FairEval conclusions across six real-world datasets and six hosted LLM families, with FairSynth-360 as a separately analyzed controlled sanity benchmark and a separately reported two-model local white-box replication stratum, under prompt/cue formulations, candidate order, ranking cutoffs, and repeated generations?
\item[RQ4:] \textbf{Personalization-preserving mitigation.} Can instruction-based and counterfactual re-ranking interventions reduce harmful identity-conditioned gaps while preserving overall utility and beneficial personality-driven personalization?
\end{description}

Our contributions are therefore not simply a larger model sweep. They are (i) a consequence-aware reformulation of fairness auditing, (ii) psychometrically grounded personality controls, (iii) a reliability protocol spanning prompts, cues, order, models, domains, and stochastic generations, and (iv) mitigation evaluated by whether it reduces harmful gaps \emph{without collapsing useful personalization}. We make no empirical claim that a particular model is fairer or that personality improves recommendation until the frozen experiments support it.

Figure~\ref{fig:framework} uses the matched-context motivating pattern familiar from counterfactual LLM-recommendation auditing~\cite{zhang2023fairllm}, but changes the interpretation: a ranking shift is treated first as sensitivity, and only preference-conditioned consequence evidence can support a harmful-disparity claim.

\section{Related Work}
\subsection{Fairness in LLM-Based Recommendation}
FaiRLLM established an early benchmark for sensitive-attribute effects in ChatGPT recommendations \cite{zhang2023fairllm}. UP5 studies fairness-aware foundation-model recommendation and proposes counterfactually fair prompting \cite{hua2024up5}. Item-side fairness has also been studied for LLM recommenders with fairness-aware calibration \cite{jiang2024itemfair}, while implicit ranking work shows that even non-sensitive profile cues can induce discriminatory ranking and evaluates fairness-aware augmentation \cite{xu2024implicit}. FairEvalLLM broadens auditing with counterfactual scenarios and extensive prompt/profile construction variants \cite{deldjoo2024fairevalllm}. CFaiRLLM moves evaluation toward consumer utility by warning that ranking differences need not be bias when they reflect true preferences \cite{deldjoo2025cfairllm}. Other recent work studies multi-domain recommendation bias and prompt intervention \cite{sakib2024challenging}, uses LLMs as fairness recognizers inside a utility-aware recommendation pipeline \cite{liu2025fairnessidentification}, and extends LLM fairness auditing to a high-stakes job-recommendation setting with user- and recruiter-side views \cite{hu2025fairwork}. FairEval treats these distinctions as prior knowledge rather than claiming them individually as new.

\subsection{Identity, Persona Cues, and Prompt Reliability}
Identity-conditioned recommendation is difficult because personalization and stereotyping can produce superficially similar output changes. Kantharuban et al. show that user identity significantly affects chatbot recommendations and that racial stereotypes can appear under explicit and implicit identity cues \cite{kantharuban2025stereotype}. Neplenbroek et al. show that LLMs infer demographic information from subtle cues and that implicit personalization can reduce response quality for minority users \cite{neplenbroek2025reading}. Persona prompting itself is also a source of variation: Lutz et al. systematically study sociodemographic persona construction \cite{lutz2025persona}, while Weeber et al. compare multiple cue forms across several LLMs and find that cue choice can change measured personalization and bias \cite{weeber2026cues}. Multi-prompt evaluation and newer prompt-sensitivity studies further caution against conclusions based on one arbitrary wording \cite{mizrahi2024multiprompt,hua2025promptsensitivity,liu2026promptsensitivity}. These findings motivate FairEval's pre-registered prompt and cue robustness analyses.

\subsection{Personality-Aware Recommendation and Psychometric Grounding}
Personality-aware recommendation predates LLMs. The GroupLens Personality 2018 resource links recommender behavior and satisfaction to measured personality \cite{nguyen2018personality}; music recommendation research provides BFI/BFI-2 profiles, ratings, and lower-order facets \cite{klec2023bigfive}; and REASONER includes short-video interactions with a 15-item Big Five instrument \cite{chen2023reasoner}. Personality has also been incorporated directly into conversational recommendation, for example in the prompt-based PPPG-DialoGPT framework \cite{elourajini2023pppg}. PerFairX studies the fairness--personality tension in LLM recommendations across movie and music domains \cite{sah2025perfairx}.

Adjacent LLM-personality work is methodologically important because it shows why personality context requires external grounding. PersonaLLM evaluates whether prompted LLM personas express assigned Big Five traits \cite{jiang2024personallm}; other work studies the stability of simulated Big Five behavior \cite{sorokovikova2024big5}; BIG5-CHAT replaces purely descriptive prompting with human-grounded personality data \cite{li2025big5chat}; and Persona-E2 reports that human-grounded personality information can reduce superficial ``personality illusion'' in downstream responses \cite{yang2026personae2}. These studies do not answer FairEval's recommendation-fairness RQs directly, but they support a key design distinction: \emph{simulated persona expression is not equivalent to measured user psychometrics}. FairEval therefore requires dataset-native measured personality and tests its user-specific value against whole-profile shuffling and one-trait observed-value controls.

\section{Problem Formulation}
Let user $u$ have observed preference history $H_u$, auditable candidate set $C_u$, and held-out relevance labels $Y_u \subseteq C_u$. Let $z_u$ denote optional user context. An LLM recommender $M$ is stochastic and induces a distribution over rankings,
\begin{equation}
R_{u}^{z,s} \sim p_M(R \mid H_u,C_u,z,t,s),
\end{equation}
where $t$ is a frozen prompt template and $s$ indexes repeated generations or provider-supported randomization.

Let $U(R,Y)$ be a conventional recommendation-utility function such as nDCG@K or Recall@K. Let $D(R,R')$ measure behavioral ranking change, such as $1-\mathrm{RBO}$ or $1-\mathrm{Jaccard}$. Crucially, $D$ is a \emph{sensitivity diagnostic}, not a fairness metric by itself.

For a paired demographic intervention $a\rightarrow a'$ that leaves $H_u$, $C_u$, $t$, and generation settings fixed, we define the signed per-user Counterfactual Utility Gap,
\begin{equation}
\CUG_u(a,a')=U(R_u^{a},Y_u)-U(R_u^{a'},Y_u).
\end{equation}
We report the signed paired distribution, absolute gap, confidence interval, and effect size rather than reducing the experiment to one list-similarity number. A large ranking shift with improved held-out utility is not treated as evidence of harm; a systematic identity-conditioned utility loss is a stronger fairness concern and is interpreted together with group-level evidence.

Where reliable item-group metadata exists, discounted exposure distributions yield a Counterfactual Exposure Gap $\CEG$. Group Utility Disparity $\GUD$ summarizes pre-specified group differences in held-out utility. Invalid Output Disparity $\IOD$ treats persistent generation failures as observable behavior rather than silently discarding them.

For measured personality, let $p_u$ be the user's true Big Five vector and $\pi(p)_u$ a profile shuffled from another user under a frozen matching/randomization scheme. We define Personality Value Added,
\begin{equation}
\PVA_u=U(R_u^{p_u},Y_u)-U(R_u^{\pi(p)_u},Y_u).
\end{equation}
Positive aggregate $\PVA$ indicates that the measured profile provides user-specific value beyond merely adding personality-shaped context. We additionally intervene on one Big Five dimension at a time while keeping the remaining measured profile fixed.

\section{Benchmark and Evaluation Design}
\subsection{Datasets}
The primary empirical benchmark contains six real-world datasets. Three provide measured psychometric information, two support controlled observed-demographic counterfactuals, and MIND supplies candidate-constrained news-domain generalization. Exact release identities, terms, hashes, filtering counts, and split/candidate-generation hashes are frozen in repository manifests before a paid pilot; third-party raw files are never substituted silently.

We additionally include \textbf{FairSynth-360}, a project-generated 360-user controlled stress-test dataset with 120 synthetic items. Its A/B/C identity label is semantically meaningless, exactly balanced, and generated independently of ground-truth relevance. A synthetic OCEAN-like vector is partially informative about the latent preference function so the same true-versus-shuffled logic can be sanity-checked under known ground truth. These quantities are \emph{synthetic controls, not observations of human demographics or measured human personality}, and FairSynth results are never pooled with RQ1/RQ2 real-world estimates.

MIND contains anonymized behavior rather than observed demographic identity. Therefore FairEval makes no observed-demographic fairness claim from MIND. Across all real datasets, we never infer protected attributes from names, free text, embeddings, ZIP codes, or model guesses. Dataset cards distinguish observed, derived, and counterfactual fields.

\subsection{Candidate-Constrained Tasks}
Open-ended requests for arbitrary movies, songs, or news confound fairness with model memorization, hallucination, item availability, and popularity. Each benchmark instance instead contains a preference history, an auditable candidate set, and held-out relevant items. Candidates are generated without an LLM and frozen before prompting. The model must return exactly $K$ unique candidate IDs in structured JSON. The primary cutoff is $K=10$, with $K\in\{5,10,20\}$ as a sensitivity analysis.

For logged-impression datasets such as MIND, the candidate set follows the observed impression task. For rating/listening datasets, held-out positives are combined with deterministic hard or popularity-matched negatives according to a dataset-specific adapter. Candidate generation hashes and split hashes are stored so all LLMs see identical tasks.

\subsection{Controlled Context Conditions}
The primary structured prompt keeps field names and field order fixed. Missing context is represented explicitly as \texttt{unspecified}; a counterfactual does not add or delete unrelated prompt sections. Conditions include preference-only ($C_0$), observed demographics when available ($C_1$), paired demographic counterfactuals ($C_2$), true measured personality ($C_3$), shuffled personality ($C_4$), one-trait personality counterfactuals ($C_5$), and a pre-specified intersectional condition ($C_6$) only on datasets that support it. $C_4$ uses a deterministic whole-profile derangement: no user receives their own profile, while the cohort's complete multivariate personality distribution and trait covariance are preserved exactly. $C_5$ changes one trait using a deterministic distant observed-value donor while holding the other four measured traits fixed; no artificial 0/1 or out-of-instrument personality extremes are fabricated. Personality is serialized from measured numeric scores and dataset-native instrument metadata; FairEval never fabricates adjectives such as ``introverted engineer.''

\subsection{Prompt, Cue, and Candidate-Order Controls}
Prompting is part of the experimental design, not post-hoc tuning. RQ1--RQ3 use a neutral audit system instruction that contains no fairness coaching. RQ4 evaluates a separate identity-irrelevance instruction as an explicit mitigation; using that instruction in the audit baseline would contaminate the measurement.

The main run uses one frozen structured task template. On a pre-registered robustness subset, we compare three semantically matched task paraphrases while keeping the JSON schema and evidence fixed. A separate cue analysis expresses the \emph{same} demographic values as structured key--value fields, a deterministic first-person disclosure, or a deterministic profile sentence; no names, implied identities, or LLM-generated persona text are used. This separates task-wording sensitivity from demographic-cue sensitivity, following concerns raised by recent persona-prompt studies \cite{lutz2025persona,weeber2026cues}.

Candidate position is also controlled. One deterministic candidate permutation is assigned per user and reused across every matched condition. Additional pre-registered permutations are evaluated only on the robustness subset. Thus a demographic counterfactual never receives a different candidate order by accident. Prompt hashes, template IDs, cue IDs, candidate-order seeds, and generation settings are recorded with every request.

\subsection{Model Panel, Gateway, Budget, and Stochasticity}
The primary cross-vendor panel freezes one hosted configuration from six independent model families while routing requests through one audited Zhizengzeng OpenAI-compatible gateway. The frozen gateway model IDs are \texttt{gpt-5.6-terra}, \texttt{claude-sonnet-5}, \texttt{gemini-3.8-flash}, \texttt{deepseek-v4.1-flash}, \texttt{qwen3.8-2.4t-a95b}, and \texttt{llama-4-maverick}. A live \texttt{GET /v1/models} preflight on the experiment key is required before paid execution; if an exact frozen identifier is absent, the experiment is versioned again rather than silently substituting a nearby model. The common gateway fixes endpoint/key provenance but is not claimed to reproduce each vendor's native serving stack or control surface exactly. This panel is intended for family diversity, not as a controlled model-size leaderboard.

A separate full-scale local white-box stratum freezes Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct \cite{qwen25tech} and Phi-3.5-mini-instruct, whose family is documented by the Phi-3 technical report \cite{phi3tech}, to exact Hugging Face revisions. The controlled FairSynth campaign contains 12,960 local generations (360 users $\times$ six registered conditions $\times$ three seeded repetitions $\times$ two models). Once exact third-party freezes are available, the same panel replicates the executable real-world RQ1/RQ2 core, registered RQ3 prompt/cue/order/cutoff/stochasticity factors, and RQ4 mitigation path. Local evidence is reported as a distinct replication stratum rather than pooled with hosted-family effects; token log-probability, NLL, perplexity, and top1--top2 margin are auxiliary uncalibrated diagnostics, not probability-of-correctness estimates.

For direct ranking, FairEval requests a low-variance generation profile and no chain-of-thought output. Because the six families are served through one OpenAI-compatible gateway, provider-native reasoning/thinking switches are treated as requested study-level policies rather than assumed native-API semantics. We log the requested model ID, returned/resolved model string, gateway provider, request timestamp, temperature/top-$p$ request, output-token field, prompt hash, candidate-order identifier, response hash, and code commit for every cell. We make no claim of exact decoding-mechanics equivalence across model families. The main evaluation uses three generations per prompt, and a frozen subset receives ten generations for RQ3 stochasticity analysis.

Paid hosted execution is governed by a pre-registered operational budget that is independent of observed outcomes: a 200 RMB normal stop target, a 250 RMB client-side emergency stop threshold, and a 2 RMB pre-request safety reserve. The runner records the initial Zhizengzeng account balance and reconciles experiment spend from balance movement before and after every persisted cell. FairEval does not represent the 250 RMB threshold as an atomic provider-side spending cap; ordinary execution intentionally stops around 200 RMB and leaves roughly 50 RMB of operational headroom for an in-flight request or the single permitted format-only repair. Once remaining experiment budget to the normal target is at or below the reserve, no new request is launched. Execution order is deterministic and fixed by the immutable plan; budget exhaustion therefore truncates coverage rather than selectively choosing cells based on interim results. Any incomplete family/dataset coverage is reported explicitly and is not treated as a complete confirmatory panel.

\subsection{Metrics and Statistical Analysis}
Recommendation effectiveness is measured primarily by nDCG@10 and Recall@10. RBO and Jaccard quantify behavioral change only. Fairness analyses report paired $\CUG$, $\GUD$, $\CEG$ where item metadata supports a defensible exposure definition, and $\IOD$. Primary $\CEG$ is computed only when every top-$K$ item has auditable group metadata; incomplete coverage is reported explicitly and is not silently renormalized. Exploratory partial-metadata exposure analysis, if used, is labeled separately. Personality analysis reports $\PVA$ and trait-stratified effects. The original PAFS is retained only as a legacy sensitivity diagnostic and is not the headline fairness estimand.

We pre-specify user as the primary unit of inference. Repeated generations are averaged within a user-condition before pairing. Persistent invalid output after the one permitted format-only repair receives zero nDCG/Recall/MRR in the primary end-to-end system analysis because no usable recommendation was delivered; valid-only utility is reported only as a labeled sensitivity analysis. $\IOD$ is analyzed as its own paired user-level outcome rather than being hidden inside utility. The inference stack uses paired bootstrap confidence intervals, paired sign-flip permutation tests as the primary matched test, Wilcoxon signed-rank sensitivity analysis with matched rank-biserial effect size, and Holm correction within pre-registered RQ$\times$metric$\times$contrast families. Prompt, cue, candidate-order, model, dataset, and generation variation are reported rather than collapsed into a single mean when they materially alter the conclusion.

\input{rq_design_table}

\subsection{Output Validation}
Every response is parsed against the same schema and checked for exact $K$, uniqueness, and frozen candidate membership. The raw response is always retained and cryptographically hashed. At most one format-only repair is allowed; it may serialize existing choices but may not add, remove, replace, or reorder them. If repair succeeds, the authoritative repaired JSON is separately hashed and the final ranking must match it exactly. Persistent failures remain outcomes, receive zero primary system utility, and contribute to $\IOD$; they are never repeatedly regenerated until a valid answer appears. Run-log auditing additionally checks immutable plan linkage, requested versus applied deliberation/sampling semantics, candidate-order/cutoff agreement, code commit, and provider token-field semantics before any statistical analysis.

\section{Mitigation: Preference-Aligned Identity Re-ranking}
RQ4 compares three interventions: (i) the unmitigated audit prompt; (ii) identity-irrelevance prompting, motivated by prior counterfactually fair prompting work \cite{hua2024up5}; and (iii) a lightweight re-ranker, \textbf{PAIR} (Preference-Aligned Identity Re-ranking).

For item $i$, let $b(i)$ be normalized rank support under preference-only evidence, let $r_a(i)$ be support under the focal demographic context $a$, and let $A$ denote the pre-registered identity contexts. Contextual PAIR is
\begin{align}
\mathrm{Fit}_{a}(i) &= \alpha b(i)+(1-\alpha)r_a(i),\\
\mathrm{CFInstability}(i) &= \operatorname{Var}_{a'\in A}[r_{a'}(i)],\\
\mathrm{PAIR}_{a}(i) &= \mathrm{Fit}_{a}(i)-\lambda\,\mathrm{CFInstability}(i).
\end{align}
Candidates are sorted by $\mathrm{PAIR}_{a}(i)$. This focal-context form intentionally avoids an identity-averaged output whose counterfactual disparity would be zero by construction. Hyperparameters $\alpha$ and $\lambda$ are selected on validation users only; test users never choose an operating point. PAIR requires at least two identity-conditioned rankings. We report a utility--fairness Pareto frontier rather than selecting a post-hoc configuration that makes one method look best. A mitigation is considered useful only if it reduces harmful gaps without erasing overall utility or beneficial true-versus-shuffled personality value.

These results are not pooled with RQ1/RQ2. The six hosted families provide a budget-bounded black-box sanity layer, while the two frozen local models execute the complete 12,960-generation FairSynth matrix and, after exact real-world freezes exist, replicate the executable RQ1--RQ4 protocol. \section{Discussion, Limitations, and Ethical Scope}
FairEval identifies controlled recommendation disparities; it does not by itself establish unlawful discrimination or user-perceived harm. Counterfactual identity edits are benchmark interventions, not claims that identity is socially interchangeable. A systematic held-out utility loss under a matched identity intervention is stronger evidence of harmful behavior than list change alone, but causal interpretation still depends on the dataset and context.

Measured personality introduces separate ethical concerns: psychographic information can improve personalization but may also enable manipulation or intrusive profiling. The study therefore tests whether personality provides incremental predictive value and does not argue that production systems should collect personality by default. We do not infer missing personality or protected attributes.

The six real-world datasets vary in age, sparsity, domains, licenses, and available user metadata. FairSynth-360 trades ecological realism for known control over the latent relevance function and is therefore a sanity test, not evidence about human demographic fairness. The six hosted model configurations differ substantially in parameter scale, post-training, and model-family behavior even though requests share one gateway; the shared gateway controls endpoint provenance but does not make the underlying models experimentally identical. The two-model local white-box campaign is a required but separately reported replication stratum: its recommendation-level effects can replicate hosted study questions, whereas its internal token-score diagnostics remain descriptive auxiliary evidence and are never pooled with hosted models that do not expose the same signals. API-hosted models and gateway routing may change over time, which makes exact model-list preflight, returned-model metadata, timestamps, and code/provenance logging essential. Candidate-constrained ranking improves evaluability but differs from unconstrained conversation, so results do not automatically transfer to every conversational recommendation setting. Finally, the 250 RMB value is only a client-side emergency stop threshold, not an atomic provider-side spending cap: the runner normally stops around 200 RMB, reconciles balance around each persisted cell, and reports any budget-truncated coverage as missing planned coverage rather than positive or negative evidence.

For an IR-for-Good framing, the intended intervention path is concrete: detect preference-irrelevant identity effects with an auditable benchmark; separate them from beneficial personalization; expose model-, domain-, and prompt-specific failure modes; and test mitigations that reduce harmful disparities while preserving relevance. Each link in that mechanism is evaluated rather than assumed.

\section{Conclusion}
FairEval redesigns fairness evaluation for personality-aware LLM recommendation around a central principle: a changed recommendation is not automatically an unfair recommendation. By combining held-out preference utility, controlled demographic counterfactuals, measured Big Five profiles, matched negative controls, repeated generations, prompt/cue/order robustness, six real-world datasets, FairSynth-360 controlled sanity tests, a six-family hosted model panel, and a separately reported full-scale two-model local white-box replication stratum, the study is designed to distinguish beneficial personalization, harmless sensitivity, and harmful identity-conditioned disparities. Final empirical conclusions are inserted only after the frozen pipeline has generated and validated the corresponding evidence.
